chapters.title: Why Each One Should Eat His Own Turtles: Equality in Uncertainty
chapters.sourcePressure: The opening fairness test: a person who sells, advises, recommends, or imposes a choice should not be able to hand the downside to someone else while keeping private certainty or upside.
chapters.coreMove: Test any recommendation by asking whether the person shaping the choice will eat the downside if it goes bad.
chapters.commonMisread: Flattening the lesson into generic honesty or nice dealing, instead of asymmetry in who knows and who pays.

chapters.title: The Most Intolerant Wins: The Dominance of the Stubborn Minority
chapters.sourcePressure: A tiny intransigent minority can set a default for everyone when the majority is flexible enough to accept the stricter option.
chapters.coreMove: Separate head-count power from tolerance asymmetry, then look for the local threshold where the strict preference becomes the whole system default.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the lesson as simple praise for stubbornness or as a majority-versus-minority politics slogan.

chapters.title: How to Legally Own Another Person
chapters.sourcePressure: Employment, status perks, and dependence can create practical ownership even when a person remains formally free.
chapters.coreMove: Distinguish formal freedom from practical freedom by locating what the institution can threaten if the person disobeys.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into a loose rant about jobs or a literal claim that employment equals slavery.

chapters.title: The Skin of Others in Your Game
chapters.sourcePressure: People often compromise because institutions can punish dependents, families, colleagues, or reputations around them.
chapters.coreMove: Before judging courage, map whose security the actor would burn by telling the truth.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the lesson generic whistleblower sympathy instead of indirect downside transfer.

chapters.title: Life in the Simulation Machine
chapters.sourcePressure: Model-driven understanding becomes suspect when the person designing the model does not absorb the cost of its errors.
chapters.coreMove: Make every abstraction prove where it touches reality and who pays when the model is wrong.
chapters.commonMisread: Attacking models as such, instead of attacking no-consequence models that outrun field correction.

chapters.title: The Intellectual Yet Idiot
chapters.sourcePressure: Credentialed experts become dangerous when their theories govern other people while the experts remain insulated from consequences.
chapters.coreMove: Discount expertise when the expert's downside is missing and the practitioner's correction loop is stronger.
chapters.commonMisread: Writing a generic anti-intellectual complaint rather than a consequence-based credibility test.

chapters.title: Inequality and Skin in the Game
chapters.sourcePressure: Taleb separates inequality earned under shared downside from inequality protected by privilege and loss transfer.
chapters.coreMove: Judge inequality by whether the winners stayed exposed to the risks that produced their rewards.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into generic inequality is bad or meritocracy is good.

chapters.title: An Expert Called Lindy
chapters.sourcePressure: Time becomes a credibility test in uncertain domains because survival under repeated stress reveals what a fresh argument cannot.
chapters.coreMove: Use endurance as evidence, without confusing age alone with truth.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating Lindy as nostalgia or automatic respect for old things.

chapters.title: Surgeons Should Not Look like Surgeons
chapters.sourcePressure: Professional theater can mislead trust when appearance becomes a substitute for competence under consequence.
chapters.coreMove: Look past polished signals and ask which evidence actually connects the person to successful performance under risk.
chapters.commonMisread: Making it about sloppy dress versus polished dress instead of cosmetic signal versus tested competence.

chapters.title: Only the Rich Are Poisoned: The Preferences of Others
chapters.sourcePressure: Status and wealth can detach people from firsthand preference and make them vulnerable to desires manufactured by others.
chapters.coreMove: Interrogate whether a preference came from direct use or from status pressure imported into your life.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the chapter as envy of luxury or simple anti-consumerism.

chapters.title: Facta non Verba (Deeds Before Words)
chapters.sourcePressure: Words become weak evidence when action under cost would reveal conviction more reliably.
chapters.coreMove: Audit sincerity by asking what the person actually does when talk would become expensive.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing the chapter to actions speak louder than words without exposure, sacrifice, or revealed preference.

chapters.title: The Facts Are True, the News Is Fake
chapters.sourcePressure: A narrative can distort judgment while each selected fact remains technically true.
chapters.coreMove: Separate the raw event from the selection, salience, and frame that made it feel like the whole reality.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into generic media outrage or claims that facts do not matter.

chapters.title: The Merchandising of Virtue
chapters.sourcePressure: Virtue display becomes suspect when the speaker gains reputation while someone else bears the cost of the moral position.
chapters.coreMove: Test moral claims by tracing who pays, who is praised, and who receives the transferred downside.
chapters.commonMisread: Writing a broad hypocrisy complaint instead of reputational arbitrage under moral cover.

chapters.title: Peace, Neither Ink nor Blood
chapters.sourcePressure: Declared peace is weak unless the arrangement gives each side a credible reason not to break it.
chapters.coreMove: Judge peace by the structure of consequence that keeps it alive after the ink dries.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the chapter generic diplomacy advice or glorifying force.

chapters.title: They Don't Know What They Are Talking About When They Talk About Religion
chapters.sourcePressure: Detached outsiders misread religion when they treat it as propositions rather than embedded practice, ritual, and function.
chapters.coreMove: Interpret a belief system through what practitioners do, risk, and repeat, not only through literal statements.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into theology, culture-war commentary, or outsider sneering.

chapters.title: No Worship Without Skin in the Game
chapters.sourcePressure: Belief becomes legible through worship, sacrifice, and cost-bearing practice rather than statements alone.
chapters.coreMove: Look for what the believer gives up or risks before treating belief as real commitment.
chapters.commonMisread: Writing devotional uplift or generic sincerity advice.

chapters.title: Is the Pope Atheist?
chapters.sourcePressure: Stated doctrine can be less informative than institutional action and revealed preference under consequence.
chapters.coreMove: Read belief by behavior under exposure while avoiding cheap accusation as the main point.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the provocative title a hypocrisy takedown instead of a revealed-preference test.

chapters.title: How to Be Rational About Rationality
chapters.sourcePressure: Rationality should be judged by survival and action under real constraints, not only by verbal coherence or formal elegance.
chapters.coreMove: Ask whether a belief or action preserves the agent under exposure before calling it irrational.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the chapter into generic decision theory or anti-reason posturing.

chapters.title: The Logic of Risk Taking
chapters.sourcePressure: Risk must be judged through ruin, leverage, and nonlinear downside rather than exciting upside or bravery stories.
chapters.coreMove: Refuse any risk whose downside can end future participation, no matter how attractive the upside looks.
chapters.commonMisread: Making the ending motivational risk-taking advice instead of ruin-sensitive judgment.
